anchor: Bred from three first-generation candidates: c7 (Levin and Brain, Code as Creative Medium: every chapter a brief with precedents, a closed exercise and an open make; the AI drafter in week one; the public sculpture as the end), c3 (Reas, McWilliams and LUST, Form+Code: parts named by what code does to form, Parameterize as a strand, the collage room and first export in week one, two tables of contents) and c4 (Klee's Pedagogical Sketchbook in drag, the application's own model: the point's walk as the opening arc, the scene tree's parent-to-child command taught and then inverted by inverse kinematics). The ordering device is the Processing Handbook's numbered returns: the spine is the index, not the order.
title: Walk, Repeat, Stand, Grow: a middle-ground course for Ada
thesis: This course starts where Klee's Pedagogical Sketchbook starts: a point that goes for a walk and becomes a line, a record, and a plane you can stand on. Then one rule makes many bodies, a seed disturbs them, joints articulate them, a sine lays their time into space, and your body becomes a class: a family of possible bodies with one axis you can argue about. With a family in hand you give it surfaces (colour, tile, pixel, noise), then forces (the walker that carried you is opened, gravity is written by hand, legs let the passive part drive), then fields that decide what the picture hides, then rules that grow. It ends by leaving the lab: failure before futures, and your family placed in a shared museum where others may change it. The order relates to Ada's spine without being forced by it. Every chapter names the spine sequence it walks and is numbered inside it ('Randomness 1' at chapter 11, 'Randomness 2' at chapter 24, 'Randomness 3' at chapter 38), so you mostly walk Ada's halls in the spine's order. Where you meet a hall early, the chapter says why you need it now (chance right after the first grid, noise as your first ground, the model that drafts your code in week one), and when the sequence comes back, the chapter says it is a return. In every chapter you build a body, turn it into a family, write down before rendering which two members will look most alike, say in one sentence what the comparison shows, write what the approximation owes or hides, and put the body where someone meets it.

parts.title: One body: point, line, plane (Code and form)
parts.promise: From an instruction to a plane you walked and can stand on, with a scanned body beside it in the headset and a drafted body checked by you: the engine calls you, everything is an object, a line is a record, a surface has a side.

parts.title: Many bodies: repeat, disturb, articulate, parameterize
parts.promise: One rule makes a floor; a seed disturbs it; joints make an organism whose parent commands its child; a sine lays time into space and sound; and your body becomes a class whose exported axis is a family you can argue about.

parts.title: Surfaces that argue: colour, tile, pixel, noise (Visualize 1)
parts.promise: Colour as a path through a space, a tile as a truth table, the same rule per body, per texel and per pixel, and noise as chance that remembers its neighbour: a ground for your family.

parts.title: Bodies under force: flow, walk, fall, reach, stand (Simulate 1)
parts.promise: The walker that carried you is opened; you write gravity yourself, extend your reach with a ray, invert the command chain with legs, and build a small complete round about standing despite every possibility of falling.

parts.title: Fields that decide what the picture hides (Visualize 2)
parts.promise: A ground others can repair, a skin a threshold extracts, a skin a shader fakes, and a floor a classifier paints: four fields, four things each picture hides.

parts.title: Rules that grow: bodies and worlds that make themselves (Simulate 2)
parts.promise: Neighbour rules, Turing's pattern on two buffers, recursion you stop, grammars that walk, bodies bred from files, and a generated world navigated as a graph.

parts.title: Leaving the lab: failure before futures
parts.promise: Soft and collective bodies measured against the headset, then the model's limits (one standpoint, a third truth value, your own prediction error as entropy) before your family stands in the shared museum under an edit rule.

tracks.title: Three weeks: a family in drag, in your own hall
tracks.length: 3 weeks, 15 days, in the Queer 3D format. Week 1 (Code and form, headset from day 2): Mon d3_01+d3_02, Tue d3_03+d3_04, Wed d3_05+d3_06 (the six runnable /course kits, two a day), Thu d3_08 (scan day, then a Quest export), Fri d3_09 (the AI drafter). Week 3: mini project; Tue d3_37 as a guest critique session walked without compulsory code (Code Societies format), Wed a second critique on the blob aesthetic walked in Noise_Space_10 and ISO_Metaballs, Fri the showing. Supplied and named because the short track skips them: heightfield_skin.gd (SurfaceTool mesh plus collider, which the long track writes in d3_07 and d3_18), the normal display in Color_Flashlight, the sweep_sheet scene, the walker and the XR rig.
tracks.mini_project: A FAMILY IN DRAG. One class of your own with one exported axis of 3-5 values (or the organism's joint axis), a prediction of the closest pair written before rendering, the comparison still from the sweep sheet, one claim sentence and a debt comment in the code. The members stand on a noise ground in your hall beside one scanned or sculpted body; one member is drafted by an AI under the three-line protocol (what should change, what must not, what observation would prove it wrong) and checked. Exported to the headset or a classmate's laptop and shown on day 15. Prompts to choose from: Virtual Creature, Parametric Object, Extrapolated Body, Personal Prosthetic (Levin and Brain), or 'the body the scanner could not see'.

tracks.title: One year: from an instruction to a public body
tracks.length: About 40 sessions over two terms, one chapter per session. Each part closes with a synthesis (d3_08, d3_14, d3_18, d3_24, d3_28, d3_34, d3_39) followed by a pause session with no new code where the year allows (Aesthetic Programming's rhythm). Term 1 ends with the midterm round (d3_24). The final brief is written at d3_37, two units before the end, and shown at d3_39.
tracks.mini_project: Midterm (d3_24): a round in your hall that a visitor can lose and replay, with a start, one way to fail, a score, a sound and a restart, saved to user://. Final (d3_39): your family placed in the class's collective museum hall with its prediction, comparison still, claim, debt comment and edit rule, walked in the headset from an exported build (the Nature of Code Ecosystem Project turned into a museum room).

chapters.title: Day Zero: the instruction is the work
chapters.body: A LeWitt location drawing turned into one body: in the supplied base scene (floor, light, Label3D) you type one line that calls a supplied place_at(where) and a cube appears at 'corner', 'midpoint' or 'centre'; one print() writes your instruction to the Output panel.

argument.axis: wording of the instruction
argument.predict: 'midpoint' and 'centre' will look most alike from the fixed camera (on a square floor both land on the middle line); 'somewhere near the middle' will not run at all, so it has no picture.
argument.claim: An instruction a partner can interpret is not one the engine can run: ambiguity shows up as an error, not as a variation.

chapters.debt: LeWitt's drafters interpreted; the engine refuses. Literalness is the price of repeatability, and it is the first algorithmic debt the course names. chapters.body: A column that grows: its height is a variable set once in _ready() and increased by h += 0.01 in _process(); a Label3D beside it prints the frame count. The delta parameter is visible in the signature and deliberately unused.

argument.axis: frame rate the scene runs at (--fixed-fps), height after five seconds
argument.predict: 90 and 120 will look most alike (heights 4.5 m and 6 m, a ratio of 4:3); 30 is half of 60. A body grown per frame is a different body on every device.
argument.claim: Growth counted in frames belongs to the machine: the headset at 90 Hz grows a column 1.5 times taller than a laptop at 60 Hz in the same five seconds.

chapters.debt: A frame is not a second, and the device decides how many there are, so the refresh rate becomes part of the body. The repair (delta) is held back on purpose until chapter 12, and the sketchbook says so. Headless runs draw no frames at all (an Ada trap), so a rule that counts frames behaves differently there.

chapters.body: A carried point that writes its own Vector3 beside itself, twice: global_position and position. A second point is placed at an expression of the first (a + Vector3.UP, a * 0.5). argument.axis: which axis the same length goes into
argument.predict: x and z will look most alike from a standing eye; y will not, because up is the direction your body has.

chapters.debt: Y-up, metres and handedness are conventions baked into every later body. VR adds a default floor height and an eye height that assume a standing adult (Bagnall on normativity in hardware, Queer Game Studies [mem]). A transform is always relative to a parent, and whose hand is the parent is a question.

chapters.title: When things go wrong: the drafter is a model
chapters.body: Your Day Zero instruction body, drafted a second time by an AI assistant as GDScript. You write three lines before you prompt: what should change, what must not change, and one observation that would prove the code wrong. You run it, break it on purpose, step through it with breakpoints, then add static types so the editor catches what the model guessed.

argument.axis: how much the prompt fixes
argument.predict: 'vague' and 'counted' will look most alike: both come back as a default cube or capsule at the origin, because the model fills every open slot with its most common answer.
argument.claim: Where the prompt is open, the model fills in its defaults; the generated body shows the model's idea of a body, not yours.

chapters.debt: The default body and algorithmic enclosure: the assistant learned from other people's code and repeats its norms (the capsule player, the cube at the origin). ML_Generative shows a generated cloud that stays near its training cloud: the drafter samples near what it has seen. Chun's 'sourcery' again: generated source you can read is not code you know. A green run is not a check: a typed set() on a mistyped property is refused in silence (Ada's own science_screen case [V CLAUDE.md]), so the falsifying observation must be something you look at.
chapters.place: Walk ML_Generative: stand where the real and the generated clouds overlap, then where the generated cloud never goes. Your hand-made and your drafted body stand side by side in your hall.

chapters.title: The organism: pivot and swing (Klee in drag I)
chapters.body: A limb of three segments as a parent-child chain with pivots, built by a loop; each joint's angle is amplitude * sin(TAU * f * t + phase), with t += delta, the course's first body that moves by itself. The frame-rate debt from chapter 2 is repaid here.

argument.axis: where the pivot sits on each segment
argument.predict: 'at the end' and 'at one third' will look most alike after 30 degrees; 'outside' makes the chain orbit instead of bend.
argument.claim: A body's motion is decided by where its joints are, not by what its parts look like.

chapters.debt: Klee maps active, medial and passive onto brain, muscle and bone and onto male and female organs (I.9-12, per c4's reading of the Praeger text). The scene tree encodes the same command chain: the parent moves the child, never the reverse. Klee in drag starts here as a code fact, not a costume; chapter 23 inverts it.

Code as Creative Medium [V ToC via c7]: the chapter unit is an assignment with a precedent, a short closed exercise and an open make; the short track runs one chapter a day; 'When Things Go Wrong' becomes the AI drafter chapter (d3_09); Personal Prosthetic, Data Self-Portrait and Virtual Public Sculpture keep their names.

Form+Code [V themes via c3]: part names by what code does to form (Repeat, Transform, Parameterize, Visualize, Simulate) are kept as labels on the parts; Parameterize runs as a named strand across four chapters (d3_14, d3_25, d3_33, d3_35) rather than as one block, so it arrives when a family is needed and is finished when a budget is.

Klee's Pedagogical Sketchbook [per c4, which checked the 1960 Praeger text; I did not reopen it]: the opening walk (point, line, record, plane) and the body book of Part I; active/medial/passive mapped onto male and female is the exact place for 'in drag', taught at d3_12 and inverted at d3_23. Klee's order is broken on purpose twice (colour early, the pendulum as a function before gravity) and each break is declared.
10 PRINT and Nake/Nees/Molnar [V research_ccs, research_bauhaus]: regularity before randomness; chance enters as the disturbance of a grid already built (d3_11 directly after d3_10).

Aesthetic Programming [V research_ccs]: a critical theme tied to each code idea and read after making; pause weeks after each part; the final brief two units before the end; 'machine unlearning' turned on the course's own assistant (d3_09 and d3_28).
Code Societies (SFPC 2019) [V research_creative]: the short track's third week uses guest critique sessions beside the student's own making, walked in halls without compulsory code (d3_37).
Montfort, Exploratory Programming [V research_ccs]: modify before write, errors in week one, 'critique my starter programs' turned on the supplied walker when it is opened (d3_20).

Albers [V research_bauhaus]: a constrained material and a stated perceptual target; the two-colour palette in d3_10 is supplied like Color-aid paper, and every chapter's prediction names the closest pair before the render.
Chun, Programmed Visions [V contents via LEARN]: 'sourcery' sits in the debt of the first chapter that opens a supplied helper (d3_06) and again at the first generated code (d3_09).
Gaboury, Image Objects [V research_engine]: one technical object read per chapter where it bites (culling at d3_07, the GPU at d3_17, the default object at d3_20).

The Nature of Code [V]: the middle of the course (flow, forces, oscillation, agents, automata, fractals, evolution) keeps NoC's order, and the final is its Ecosystem Project turned into a museum hall.

What no comparable course gives, stated plainly [V LEARN verdict]: none combines critique, writing code, 3D or VR bodies and art-school beginners. The canon's critique is social and linguistic; the geometric and bodily debts here (polycount against deformation, the blob aesthetic, recursion that must be stopped, the one standpoint that closes an impossible figure) have almost no precedent, so the course does not borrow authority for them.
